did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with a twofold command: “Comfort, comfort my people.” The repetition emphasizes the central role of comfort in the chapter’s opening message.

The way to redemption is described as a road that must be prepared in the wilderness: valleys will be raised, mountains and hills brought low, rough places made level, and difficult terrain turned into a plain.
The purpose of preparing the way is the revelation of the LORD’s glory. According to the verse, all humanity will see it together, because the mouth of the LORD has spoken.
The chapter compares humanity and its faithfulness to grass and flowers of the field, emphasizing their temporary nature. In contrast, the word of our God stands forever.
Zion, herald of good news, and Jerusalem are called to climb a high mountain, raise their voices without fear, and proclaim to the cities of Judah: “Here is your God!”

The LORD is portrayed through two complementary images: as a mighty ruler who comes with power and reward, and as a shepherd who gathers the lambs, carries them close to his heart, and gently leads the nursing ewes.

Through rhetorical questions, the chapter describes the greatness of the Creator: he measures the waters in the hollow of his hand, the heavens by the span of his hand, and the dust of the earth by a third of a measure.
The nations and the islands are described in relation to the LORD as a drop from a bucket and dust on the scales—an expression of the Creator’s exalted status compared with the power of the nations.

The chapter emphasizes the difference between the Creator and an idol. An idol is made by a craftsman, covered with gold, and dependent on human choice and labor; therefore, it cannot represent the One who created everything.
The LORD is described as the One who brings out the host of heaven by number and calls each star by name. Because of his great power, not one of them is missing.
